section: Final fit and test set predictions
text:
Final fit and test set predictions

Fit Final Model


Code
final_fit <- workflow_obj %>% 
    fit(data = train)




Test set predictions


Code
test_preds <- predict(final_fit, new_data = test) %>% 
    bind_cols(test)




Final performance evaluation


Code
test_metrics <- test_preds %>%
  metrics(truth = quality, estimate = .pred)

test_metrics


# A tibble: 3 × 3
  .metric .estimator .estimate
  <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
1 rmse    standard       0.738
2 rsq     standard       0.272
3 mae     standard       0.577




Predictions visualized


Code
test_preds %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = .pred, y = quality)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Predicted vs Actual (Test Set)", x = "Predicted", y = "Actual") +
  theme_minimal()











Code
test_preds %>%
  mutate(residual = .pred - quality) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = .pred, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs Predicted", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal()









The RMSE was very close for the training and test data, but overall this is not an accurate model. The residual plot shows strange patterns, this model is clearly underfitting.


Model inspection


Code
lm_model <- extract_fit_parsnip(final_fit)$fit
summary(lm_model)

Most variables are statistically significant, as is the model itself. I want to point this out and emphasize it, because the “significance” doesn’t mean we have a useful model. The model doesn’t predict very well.
In the future I might try this with interactions with type - the predictor variable impact might very well depend on the type of wine. Or maybe it’s better to fit a model separately for red and white wines.


Discussion - Linear Regression
Linear regression probably isn’t the best choice for the quality rating. We could treat the rating as a categoric variable and do ordinal (multilevel) logistic regression. This is an approach I’ve taken in some projects. For this project I’ll use a random forest model and compare.
It’s worth noting that the quality rating really is a categoric scale, I’ve been treating it as a continuous number in this project. My reason for doing this, is that this is very often done in industry. I might not agree with it but it’s common. We’ll take the categoric approach in a separate project.

title: Real Time SPC - Weight Loss
text:
When you learn about SPC (statistical process control) often you see a dataset all at once. In practice though, you have to start somewhere, and continually make decisions. With each new data point, do I act (investigate, change), or leave the process alone (for now).
My goal with this project is to show a “real” SPC project from start to ongoing - once I achieve the objective I’ll switch to monitoring to maintain progress.

title: Real Time SPC - Weight Loss
text:
Starting a new control chart
To start with control charts we need some data. At work you might already have some, but for this project let’s say we don’t have any data.
I plan to track my weight weekly, because that’s a meaningful time frame to me, and easy to remember. I feel monthly isn’t often enough, if I’m progressing I want to know about it (encouraging!), and if I’m not progressing I want to know so I can change my behavior (process inputs) and drive the progress I need.
To get started I’m going to take measurements daily to get an idea of how much weight fluctuates, and start from there. Once I’ve tracked daily for awhile we will probably switch to weekly.

title: Real Time SPC - Weight Loss
text:
Run Chart to begin
To start out, I’m just going to plot each point in order as it happens (run chart).

title: Real Time SPC - Weight Loss
text:
First point
I’m not going to share my actual weights here. One great thing about a control chart is that I can create and share it, and you can view and interpret it without labeled numbers. Just the points themselves and the control limits.
Let’s look at this first point.









Our first datapoint. I can already tell you it’s not what I want. It’s far enough from my goal that one data point is enough. Let’s look at where I want to be:









Here we see the journey from where I am to where I want to be. We don’t know what it’s going to look like in between! Once I reach the goal I’ll move to maintenance tracking, it isn’t so useful to improve something then lose the progress later.

Day 2Day 3Day 4Day 5Day 6Day 7Day 8Day 9











It’s hard to tell if anything is happening yet. I set the y limits to be constant, so the y axis isn’t changing with every new dot.











Ok we are seeing some day to day variation. This is the type of variation that can be misleading! If I was weighing myself weekly or monthly and seeing this kind of variation, I might alternate between being encouraged and discouraged.
I know you can’t see the y axis scale, I’ll tell you from day 1 to day 2 the weight measurement decreased by 0.6 lbs, and from day 2 to day 3 it increased by 0.8 lbs. This variation doesn’t indicate an actual lasting change, it could be for many reasons but for the context of reaching my goal, it’s not telling me anything useful.











On day 4 the measurement went “down” again, so let’s see what day 5 holds next.











Wow! That’s pretty cool, down again, and what looks like a large decrease! Maybe a sustained decrease! It’s hard not to be encouraged by something like this. I’m gonna be crushed on day 6 if it goes back up again.











Looks like day 6 went back “up” again. This isn’t unusual for a process with variation over time. Right now we’re getting a good estimate of how much the measurement can change day to day, and about where it’s located (average).











Day 7, first week already! Seeing two consecutive points moving up might be discouraging, but again our run chart soon to be followed by control chart helps keep it in context.
Week 1 thoughts - I don’t think I’ve lost any weight yet. Or if I have, I can’t detect it yet. You can see how the day we start at can have a big impact - imagine if we had started on day 5!? With SPC we would still see the process is stable, but without SPC we might even feel we had gained…when really nothing changed.
Week 1 actions:

Keep tracking daily, for at least another week (maybe 2), to get a feel for what’s happening.
Start trying more deliberately to change the system. This brings up an important point, with SPC we want to also track relevant inputs. I’ll start logging exercise data - to assess how much I’m doing, also to motivate me to do more. If I see an empty exercise lot, I’ll be motivated to make sure it’s filled.












Day 8, back “down” a little again. I know enough to say it’s relatively stable, at least I’m not gaining, but let’s emphasize progress. Watch closely as I attempt to drive progress moving forward.











Day 9, I agree with my assessment yesterday that this process is unchanged (so far). My weight seems to be stable around the average. I know enough, I might as well start using a control chart.

title: Real Time SPC - Weight Loss
text:
First Control Limits Set (Day 9)
I’m using the values from days 1 - 9 to set my baseline or reference control limits. These will be used for the control chart moving forward. The limits represent the current state - based on what I know so far, given the data (and variation observed), I expect future values to be centered around the average, and within the limits - until something happens or changes.
If I observe a point outside the limits, I will have a potential signal that something might be different. If the point is above the upper limit it’s undesirable, it means I most likely gained weight. A point below the lower limit is desirable - this shows that I probably have actually reduced my weight.
Control charts are so valuable, because they’re going to help me not worry if it looks like I’ve gained, and they will help me know when I’m progressing in the right direction. Without the limits to put the data in context, the variation in the data makes it hard to know what’s really happening point to point.









To put this in context, our best estimate of my current weight is the blue line. The lower limit (red) is over 2 pounds less than the average.
I might say: “Given how much variation there is in the data from day to day, it will be difficult to detect a change unless it is more than 2 pounds different from where we are starting”.
I can’t reliably detect anything less than a 2 - 2.5 lb change! That’s good to know - I won’t get discouraged. It might take 1, 2, or even 3 weeks to lose that much.

Day 10Day 11Day 12Day 13Day 15Day 16Day 17











Day 10 assessment: No detectable change
Day 10 decision: evaluate inputs, try to create change











Day 11 assessment: No detectable change
Day 11 decision: evaluate inputs, try to create change
Day 11 comment: interesting to see 4 points in a row “hugging” the average. So far 7 of 11 points appear “very close” to the average, actually slightly below the average. I don’t know that this means anything.











<ScaleContinuousPosition>
 Range:  
 Limits:  243 --  249


Day 12 assessment: No detectable change
Day 12 decision: evaluate inputs, try to create change
Day 12 comment: That’s a big jump on day 12! Or it looks like a big jump. Since it’s within the control limits, I believe the weight has not actually changed yet. This is variation on display.


I was traveling these days and didn’t check in. We can work with a couple missing observations, we won’t know what happened on those days but with the control chart we’ll continue to monitor for change.











Day 15 assessment: No detectable change
Day 15 decision: evaluate inputs, try to create change. Start tracking physical activity and minutes.
Day 15 comment: Back from the holiday, time to get serious. Continue daily tracking.











Nothing much to note, keep monitoring











Day 17 assessment: This is the lowest point observed so far. It’s almost outside LCL.
Day 17 decision: Keep monitoring, keep focusing on inputs.
Day 17 comments: I won’t be surprised to see day 18 or 19 back higher again. While this point almost being outside LCL is encouraging, I want confirmation through ongoing monitoring before deciding that this represents a real change.
Can you imagine tracking something like this without a control chart or at least a run chart (put the dots in order as they are observed!)? It might be very discouraging. I have context with the chart, to see if a change is “real” or not. Another way to put it, all these points are actually real, but I want to know if they represent my goal, which is a sustained reduction.
If day 17 is a “real” decrease it will be great news. I want to point out that even if it is a real change, we don’t know when the change happened exactly. Given how much variation is present from day to day, my weight might have been slowly decreasing for awhile, we just weren’t able to detect it yet. Can’t wait to see what happens tomorrow.

title: Real Time SPC - Weight Loss
text:
Day 53 - A decision!
I can’t believe it’s been this long. I tracked some days but didn’t update the project. And my tracking trailed off you’ll see.
I didn’t intend for the project to get this real, but since it happened let’s embrace it. Here is what I have:









I can’t say what’s happened on the days with no data. But in a way it doesn’t matter for my objective, which is to drive the process downward (then keep it there).
Based on what I have there is no indication that the process has changed - there is a lot of variation, and maybe weight did change temporarily but it looks like it’s about the same as day 1.
The period from day 17 to 28 might have been a small decrease? Day 17 was just outside LCL which is the first signal, followed by most points until day 28 being below average.
Next steps - I am going to switch to weekly tracking, daily is too much to keep up with.
I will calculate weekly control limits and show how different they are than daily.
I will also try harder to make change happen.

title: About
text:
Hello!
I focus on data analysis that helps solve problems and supports good decision making. I like to “figure things out”.
I have a background in food science, product development, and manufacturing. (Every wonder how products get in a box and end up at the store? I was involved in a lot of the steps to get there.)
While I was working, I found I had an interest in statistics as a way to help solve problems, and I’ll even say a talent for it. I worked with many methods and many types of data, solving problems and helping figure things out:

finding insights to solve customer complaints - EDA, visualization, text analysis
improve manufacturing consistency - experimental design, statistical process control
develop meaningful measurements and metrics - measurement systems analysis
designing experiments for maximal effectiveness and efficiency (solving problems quickly at a fraction of the cost!) - experimental design
planning and analyzing consumer research (taste testing) to learn what drives new product liking - text analysis, multivariate analysis, clustering

I had job titles like R&D Scientist and R&D Process Engineer, but a large portion of what I did each day was data science. It had an impact too, each project I worked on involved real products, real people, real consequences.
I liked stats so much that I decided to go back to school while working full time and earned an MS in Applied Statistics in 2019. Totally worth it.
I feel my experiences have given me a unique perspective - food is relatively hands on and you can develop an intuitive sense for working with data. It’s very grounded in the “real world”, and your senses, there are a lot of connections to draw. Working in manufacturing is fast paced and filled with changes (“large” data + velocity), combined with lab experiments and consumer research (slower, “small” data) - I’ve experienced quite a combination of situations, and I’m familiar with what might work (and maybe more important what doesn’t work) in a given situation.
I took a new job focused full time on data in 2022 (corporate statistician). My position was cut in 2023 in headcount reductions so for the last 2 years I’ve been self employed. I’m looking for new opportunities - either more consulting work or a full time job. Through this portfolio I hope you can get to know me and my data mindset.

title: Welcome to My Portfolio
text:
Welcome to My Portfolio
Hi I’m Ben - a data scientist with a background in industrial statistics and food science. I have a few projects featured here, my blog contains more projects and thoughts, and soon I’ll be posting on YouTube as well. Let me know if you’d like to collaborate or hear more about a topic!
Update 8/13/25 New projects added, plus some twists in real time SPC (maybe a little too real)

Featured Project: Real Time SPC This one is really exciting. I’m using the power of Statistical Process Control (SPC) to track my fitness progress. Unlike a textbook example where you are given a dataset, this dataset is being generated in real time, day by day, week by week, and I don’t know how it’s going to go. We will find out together. Keep checking back for updates!
Wine quality Here I use the well known wine quality dataset to show some fundamental exploratory data analysis, visualization, and predictive modeling. I focus on my thought process throughout. This project uses linear regression and random forest models to predict wine quality, and I conclude with some thoughts and next steps.
Blog: My thoughts and more projects I will be adding smaller projects here, capturing my thoughts.

mypdf <- pdftools::pdf_text("annual-fatalities-1920-2021.pdf")

#split into lines
lines <- strsplit(mypdf[1], "\n")[[1]]

# remove the top title, and info lines at the bottom
lines_clean <- lines[3:which(str_detect(lines, "Source")) - 1]

# split each line apart
tokens <- str_split(lines_clean, "\\s{2,}") # split every 2 spaces seems to be the structure

# turn tokens list into dataframe
flat <- unlist(tokens)

flat <- flat[flat != ""] # remove empty space

# get the year and numbers paired in dataframe
df <- tibble(raw = flat) %>%
  mutate(group = rep(1:(n()/2), each = 2)) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(
    year = as.integer(first(raw)),
    fatalities = parse_number(last(raw))
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(year) %>% 
    drop_na() %>% 
    select(-group)
